notes.meaning: Paul now turns to questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter, starting with marriage and sex. Saying it is "good" to stay away from sexual relations does not mean marriage is wrong. It means staying single can be wise and helpful, especially in hard times. Paul may even be repeating the Corinthians' own saying, which he only partly agrees with. He sets a limit on it in the next verse.

Sexual sin was everywhere in Corinth. So Paul says marriage is God's way to guard against it. "His own wife" and "her own husband" also mean one spouse each, not several. This is not the only reason for marriage. Paul is simply answering the question in front of him.

Husband and wife owe each other the closeness of married love, including sex. The duty runs both ways. The stress is on giving to the other, not on demanding. Paul gently corrects anyone who thought living apart as if unmarried made them holier.

In marriage, each spouse has given themselves to the other, so neither acts as if their body belonged only to themselves. Paul puts husband and wife on equal footing here. This gives no excuse for forcing or abusing a spouse. It calls each one to serve the other in love, and it rules out being unfaithful or taking another partner.

Married couples should not hold back from each other. Holding back is like cheating your spouse of what you owe them. The only exception is when both agree, for a short time, to give themselves to prayer. Then they should come together again, so Satan cannot use their weakness to tempt them. Giving up married closeness for good goes against what Paul says here.

A "concession" is something allowed, not required. Paul allows the short time apart for prayer, but he does not order it. In the same way, he is not ordering every person to marry. Marriage is open to all, but no one is forced into it.

Paul wishes everyone could live single and content, as he did, free to serve God. But he knows this is a gift God gives to some and not others, just as Jesus said in Matthew 19:11. Both marriage and singleness come from God. So we should not judge others by the gift we happen to have.

Paul tells those who are single and those who are widowed that it is good to stay as they are, like him. This shows Paul was unmarried at that time. "Good" again means helpful and wise, not more holy. He explains the practical reasons later in the chapter.

If they cannot control their desires, they should marry. To "burn with passion" means to be overwhelmed by desire, not just to feel a passing temptation. Marriage is a good gift God provides for this. It is not simply the lesser of two evils. This also shows that widows are free to marry again.

To married believers, Paul passes on a command from the Lord Jesus himself (see Matthew 19). Marriage is for life. A wife must not leave her husband, and a husband must not divorce his wife. If a wife has already left, she must stay unmarried or make peace with her husband. Several of these writers note that Jesus allowed divorce for sexual unfaithfulness (Matthew 5:32).

"The rest" are people who became Christians after marrying someone who still does not believe. "I, not the Lord" means Jesus had not spoken directly about this case. It does not mean Paul's words are any less inspired, that is, any less guided by God. If the unbelieving wife is happy to stay, the Christian husband must not divorce her.

The same rule holds for a Christian wife whose husband does not believe. If he is willing to stay, she must not divorce him. She should be all the more loving and faithful, to show him how good her faith is.

A Christian need not fear being made spiritually unclean by an unbelieving spouse. "Sanctified" means set apart as holy. The unbeliever is not saved by the marriage. But because one partner belongs to God, the marriage itself is holy. Likewise, their children are not "unclean" outsiders. They are counted among God's people.

differ.view: Children with even one believing parent belong to God's covenant people, his promise-family. This supports baptizing them as infants.
The verse says nothing about baptism. "Holy" means the children were born in a proper, God-approved marriage.
A child of a believer can be regarded as saved until the child is old enough to answer to God for themselves.

notes.meaning: The believer must not start a separation. But if the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer should let them go. The believer is "not bound" in such a case, so they do not have to chase the other person or give up their faith to keep them. God has called us to peace, not to endless fighting.

differ.view: A believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is freed from the marriage and may marry again.
The deserted believer may live apart in peace, but is not free to marry someone else.

notes.meaning: You cannot know whether God may use you to bring your spouse to faith in Christ. So stay, and keep hoping and praying. A patient, loving, godly life is often what wins a husband or wife (1 Peter 3:1).

Here is the general rule. Live the life God has given you, in the situation where he called you to follow Christ. Becoming a Christian does not cancel your earthly duties and relationships. Paul teaches this same rule in every church.

Circumcision was the mark of being Jewish. A Jewish believer should not try to remove that mark. A non-Jewish believer should not get circumcised, as some false teachers were urging. Both stand equal in the church.

Outward marks like circumcision count for nothing with God. What matters is obeying God from the heart, "faith working by love." Paul is not saying we earn salvation by keeping rules. He is showing what a believer should aim at.

Each person should stay in the situation they were in when God called them, unless there is good reason to change. Paul is not forbidding all change. He is warning against restless, careless change, and teaching contentment.

If you were a slave when you came to faith, don't let it trouble you. Your standing with Christ is not lessened. But if you can lawfully gain your freedom, take the chance. Freedom is the better state.

A slave who trusts Christ is truly free, because the Lord has set him free from sin. A free person who trusts Christ now belongs to Christ as his servant. So before Christ they stand on the same level. This comforts the slave and humbles the free.

Christ bought you with the price of his own life (see 6:20). So you belong to him above any human master. Don't let anyone else rule you in a way that overrides Christ, and if you are free, don't sell yourself back into slavery.
Paul repeats his rule, adding "with God." Wherever you are in life, stay close to God and do everything as before him. His favour is not limited to any outward situation.

Now Paul speaks about unmarried people. Jesus had left no direct command about them. So Paul gives his careful judgment as one whom God, in mercy, has made a trustworthy apostle, a messenger sent by Christ. It is advice, not a command, but it still carries God-given authority.

Because of the "present crisis", the hard times and persecution Christians faced, Paul thinks it best for a person to stay as they are. Some writers see this as the troubles believers face in every age. Either way, it was not meant as a permanent rule against marriage.
If you are married, don't try to get out of it. Keep living out your marriage faithfully. If you are single, don't rush to find a wife in these hard times. Neither should seek to change their state.

Getting married is not a sin, for a man or for a young woman. But married people will face extra troubles, especially when persecution can tear families apart. Paul wants to spare them that. He gives advice, not a heavy rule.

Life is short, and this world as we know it is passing away like a changing scene on a stage. So hold earthly things loosely. Married people should love their spouses, yet stay devoted to God first. Grief and joy should both be held lightly, buying should be done as stewards rather than owners, and the world should be used without being wrapped up in it. Paul is not telling anyone to neglect their family. He is teaching that God comes first.
Paul wants them free from anxious, worrying care. An unmarried man has fewer distractions. He can give his full attention to the Lord's work and to pleasing the Lord, if he uses that freedom well.

A married man must also care for his wife and home. That is right and his duty, but it divides his attention. The same is true for women. A single woman can devote herself fully to the Lord in body and spirit, while a married woman rightly cares how to please her husband. Single life is not purer than marriage. It simply has fewer cares.

Paul says all this for their good. He is not trying to throw a noose over them and force their choice. His aim is what is fitting, and hearts that can serve the Lord without distraction. Each person stays free to marry or not.

Most older writers read this as being about a father and his unmarried daughter who is past her youth. If keeping her single seems unfair to her and she should marry, he may let them marry. That is no sin. Some read it instead as a man deciding about his own single life.

But suppose a man has firmly made up his mind, feels no pressing need, and is free to follow his own will. If he decides not to give her in marriage, he does well. Parents should weigh what is truly good for their child, not force their own wishes.

Both choices are good. Marrying is right. Not marrying is "better" only because of the hard times and the freedom it gives to serve God, not because marriage is less holy. In the end Paul leaves the choice to each case.

Marriage binds a wife to her husband for life, and only death ends it. After he dies, she is free to marry again. So second marriages are allowed. The one limit is "in the Lord": she should marry a fellow believer, in the fear of God.

In Paul's judgment, a widow will likely be happier staying single, with fewer cares to distract her. "I think that I too have the Spirit of God" is not doubt. It is a confident claim to be guided by God, perhaps a gentle answer to those in Corinth who questioned him.
